# How crawling works

Day 1, 14:05 · Cherry Prommawin, Gary Illyes, Search Relations · coverage: slides, transcript

Speakers from on-stage hand-overs between the two and the host's thanks to Gary and Cherry. Transcript from a second attendee recording; two audio recordings cover the talk except for about three minutes before the crawling infrastructure part.

## Claims

- **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
  <br><sub>`D1-C063` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works), [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D2-C024](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C026](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C048](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C127](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Extended by [D2-C167](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Extended by [D2-C441](D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** The crawler has multiple tasks: fetch from the internet, ensure it doesn't break the internet, and enforce robots.txt policies. Fetched data is sent for indexing.
  > "Ensure we don't break the internet"
  <br><sub>`D1-C064` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works), [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers) · Extended by [D2-C024](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C025](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C204](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Extended by [D2-C296](D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** The scheduler is shared infrastructure that decides what to fetch and when and sends URLs to the crawler. Each team decides the scheduling parameters for its own user agents.
  <br><sub>`D1-C065` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Crawling infrastructure](https://developers.google.com/crawling), [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D2-C706](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Extended by [D3-C385](D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand.
  <br><sub>`D1-C067` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · Extended by [D2-C189](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Extended by [D2-C427](D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-04`, `DEV-URL-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot currently fetches only the first 2MB of each URL, HTTP headers included (64MB for PDFs); bytes past that cutoff are not fetched, rendered or indexed, and each resource the page loads has its own separate limit.
  <br><sub>`D1-C136` · Search Central blog (31 March 2026) · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · is the documentation · [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post) · Used by `DEV-PRF-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Inside Googlebot post warns that bloated inline base64 images, large blocks of inline CSS or JavaScript, or megabytes of menus can push a page's text or structured data past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff, and advises moving heavy CSS and JavaScript to external files and placing meta tags, the title, the canonical and essential structured data high in the HTML.
  <br><sub>`D1-C137` · Search Central blog (31 March 2026) · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · is the documentation · [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post) · Used by `DEV-PRF-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's crawling talk opened with how the internet works (TCP/IP, internet service providers, IP addresses, URLs, DNS and HTTP), because crawling can only be understood with that wider scope.
  <br><sub>`D1-C317` · Day 1, How crawling works (Cherry Prommawin) · Repeated by [D2-C847](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A URL states how a resource is requested (the protocol, HTTP or HTTPS), where (the host, meaning which computer on the network) and what (the path to the exact page or file).
  <br><sub>`D1-C318` · Day 1, How crawling works (Cherry Prommawin) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** DNS works as the internet's address book: it is consulted for each request and tells the client at which IP address a host name can be reached.
  <br><sub>`D1-C319` · Day 1, How crawling works (Cherry Prommawin) · consistent with Google docs · [Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/dns-network-errors)</sub>

- **[Stage]** An HTTP 200 OK status only means that the server believes it managed to do what the client asked for.
  > "just means that the server believes that it managed to accomplish whatever the user was asking for"
  <br><sub>`D1-C320` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes) · Used by `DEV-ERR-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes pointed to the Last-Modified and ETag headers as the fields of an HTTP response that matter for caching.
  <br><sub>`D1-C321` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers) · Used by `DEV-SRV-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Googlebot is an ordinary HTTP client with nothing special about it: like a browser, it fetches a URL it was given and returns the fetched bytes to Google's servers.
  > "Googlebot is just a client. It is an HTTP client. There's nothing all that much special about it."
  <br><sub>`D1-C322` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post), [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works)</sub>

- **[Stage]** AI agents are, technically, the same thing as crawlers: HTTP clients that accomplish something on behalf of a user or a service.
  <br><sub>`D1-C323` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google runs probably hundreds, if not thousands, of crawlers on its crawler infrastructure; some of them are named and some are not.
  <br><sub>`D1-C324` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Googlebot is the crawler Google uses for web search, including Search's AI features.
  <br><sub>`D1-C325` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers), [Crawling infrastructure](https://developers.google.com/crawling) · Extends [D1-C038](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google does not let each team build its own crawler: its many crawlers share one crawler infrastructure, because every crawler must accomplish a few specific tasks and obey Google's internal crawling policies.
  <br><sub>`D1-C326` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Crawling infrastructure](https://developers.google.com/crawling), [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post) · Extended by [D1-C066](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said it does not usually talk publicly about crawl components such as the scheduler and the crawl queue, because the details get confusing and taken out of context.
  <br><sub>`D1-C327` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · Used by the glossary term *Crawl scheduler*</sub>

- **[Stage]** During indexing Google extracts the URLs found in fetched content and passes them back to the crawler and the scheduler to be crawled.
  <br><sub>`D1-C328` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Repeated by [D2-C048](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Apart from contractual crawlers, all of Google's automated crawlers obey robots.txt, which Google treats as the way site owners opt out of its crawling.
  <br><sub>`D1-C329` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers), [List of Google's special-case crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-special-case-crawlers) · Extended by [D1-C512](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Repeated by [D2-C848](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The only Google-owned crawlers that do not obey robots.txt are contractual crawlers, which crawl a site whose owner has agreed that Google may crawl it however it likes.
  <br><sub>`D1-C330` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [List of Google's special-case crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-special-case-crawlers), [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers) · Used by the glossary term *Contractual crawlers (special-case crawlers)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's crawl scheduler very likely deprioritises a URL when the URL or its site is known to be historically spammy.
  <br><sub>`D1-C331` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D3-C612](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The crawl scheduler logs how often each page changes and crawls frequently changing pages first: a news site's homepage, which changes very often, is prioritised over its terms of service page, which may change once a year.
  <br><sub>`D1-C332` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Used by the glossary term *Crawl scheduler*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The scheduler hands the crawler an ordered list of URLs from the crawl queue, and the crawler works through the list from top to bottom.
  <br><sub>`D1-C333` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Crawl scheduler*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Different Google teams prioritise crawling differently: web search cares a lot about the quality of a site and its content, while Ads wants to check every publisher page that wants to appear in Google Ads, so it schedules those URLs as they come in.
  <br><sub>`D1-C334` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D1-C538](D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Crawling for Gemini may be set to care less about quality and more about the amount of content, because for large language models the number of tokens matters more than quality.
  > "the number of tokens is actually more important"
  <br><sub>`D1-C335` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C039](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google finds what to crawl mainly by extracting URLs from previously crawled pages, and additionally from sitemaps.
  <br><sub>`D1-C336` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works), [Learn about sitemaps](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview) · Extends [D1-C040](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** An XML sitemap, a format from around 2005, gives Google, other search engines and potentially AI systems a list of the URLs a site wants crawled; Google called it nothing fancy but said it still uses sitemaps.
  <br><sub>`D1-C337` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Learn about sitemaps](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview), [How is a Google Sitemap different from an HTML sitemap?](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2005/09/how-is-google-sitemap-different-from) · Extended by [D3-C610](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Extended by [D3-C611](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google described its crawling as a large-scale distributed swarm of simple HTTP clients, roughly what one would get by deploying many wget or curl libraries on cloud compute instances.
  > "a large-scale distributed swarm of simple HTTP clients"
  <br><sub>`D1-C338` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** To debug crawl issues, Google points site owners to the Crawl Stats report in Search Console, found in the Settings page under Crawl stats.
  <br><sub>`D1-C339` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [Crawl Stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`, the glossary term *Crawl Stats report*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Search Console's Crawl Stats report shows how much Google crawls from a site, the errors Google received, and the content types fetched by the different crawlers.
  <br><sub>`D1-C340` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [Crawl Stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`, the glossary term *Crawl Stats report*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes called the Crawl Stats report the most valuable tool for debugging crawl errors, together with server logs, which he called the real thing for those who know how to read them.
  <br><sub>`D1-C341` · Day 1, How crawling works (Gary Illyes)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot is today just one user of a centralized crawling platform, and that dozens of other clients, such as Google Shopping and AdSense, send their crawl requests through the same infrastructure under other crawler names, with only the larger ones documented.
  > "Googlebot is just a user of something that resembles a centralized crawling platform"
  <br><sub>`D1-C342` · Search Central blog (31 March 2026) · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · is the documentation · [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's crawler documentation says special-case crawlers serve specific Google products where the crawled site and the product have an agreement about the crawl process, so they may ignore robots.txt rules; AdsBot, for example, ignores the global (*) user agent with the ad publisher's permission.
  <br><sub>`D1-C343` · Google · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · is the documentation · [List of Google's special-case crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-special-case-crawlers), [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers) · Used by the glossary term *Contractual crawlers (special-case crawlers)*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** On stage Google spoke of probably hundreds, if not thousands, of crawlers, while its Inside Googlebot post speaks of dozens of other clients; both agree that only the larger crawlers are documented, so a Google user agent missing from the public lists is not proof of a fake request, and reverse DNS or Google's published IP ranges are the test.
  <br><sub>`D1-C344` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How crawling works</sub>
